lesson.title: Dollars Instead of Bullets? Taft's Economic Foreign Policy
lesson.summary: President William Howard Taft's administration promoted American loans and investment abroad, especially in Latin America and East Asia, as a supposedly gentler alternative to Roosevelt's military interventionism, though it still relied on force when American money was threatened.
lesson.body:
When William Howard Taft succeeded Theodore Roosevelt as president in 1909, he and his Secretary of State, Philander Knox, pursued a foreign policy that came to be called dollar diplomacy. The core idea was to encourage American banks and businesses to invest in and lend money to governments in Latin America and parts of East Asia, particularly China and Manchuria. The reasoning was straightforward: if American capital, rather than European capital, funded railroads, ports, and government budgets in these regions, the United States could extend its influence and keep European and Japanese rivals out, all without the expense and controversy of sending in the Marines. Supporters described the approach as substituting dollars for bullets.

This policy shared the same underlying goal as the Roosevelt Corollary discussed earlier: keeping European powers from gaining a foothold in the Western Hemisphere and securing American economic dominance in the region. What changed was the method. Where Roosevelt had claimed an explicit right of military and political intervention, Taft's administration preferred quieter economic leverage, at least in theory. In reality, dollar diplomacy often required military backing anyway, because American investments needed protecting once they were made.

Nicaragua provides the clearest example. The United States supported opposition to Nicaraguan President Jose Santos Zelaya, who resisted American economic influence, and he was forced from power in 1909. When the country slid into further instability, the Taft administration sent U.S. Marines into Nicaragua in 1912 to protect American financial interests and the government it favored, and American forces remained involved there for years afterward. Far from avoiding intervention, dollar diplomacy often led to it, just with an economic justification layered on top. The contradiction between the peaceful rhetoric of dollar diplomacy and its coercive reality deepened resentment toward the United States across Latin America, a resentment that Woodrow Wilson would inherit, and in some ways worsen through his own interventions, when he became president in 1913.
